newsitem.title: MALI: Christopher arrives in Mali to start Africa tour.
newsitem.headline: Christopher arrives in Mali to start Africa tour.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher kicked off his first trip to sub-Saharan Africa in Mali on Monday, with a visit intended as a tribute to its progress towards democracy.

Christopher, who arrived from Israel and efforts to ease tension in the Middle East, will also visit Ethiopia, Tanzania, South Africa and Angola. He is the first U.S. secretary of state to visit sub-Saharan Africa in more than six years.
The people of Mali, hoping the visit will lead to increased U.S. aid for their impoverished West African nation, prepared a rousing welcome for him complete with traditional dance groups.

"The visit of the Secretary of State is a tribute to democracy," wrote the government daily L'Essor in an editorial, referring to Mali's smooth break with one-party dictatorship, culminating in multi-party elections in 1992.
"It can also be expected to be an opportunity for (Mali) to plead for bilateral aid to be maintained at a level compatible with persistent emergencies in Mali," it added.

U.S. officials said earlier that Christopher would use his week-long African tour to press U.S. plans to replace U.N. Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, urging African leaders to propose alternative candidates.
The Organisation of African Unity in July backed the Egyptian for a second term but made it clear Africa's ultimate concern was that the job should go to an African.
Peace in Liberia and Angola and in Burundi and the rest of the Central African Great Lakes region will also figure highly on Christopher's tour agenda.
Landlocked Mali has a population of 9.4 million people with an annual per capita income of $250. It has won plaudits from the World Bank for its economic reforms.

Assistant secretary of state George Moose, who specialises in African affairs, said earlier Christopher would "showcase the significant contribution, progress, that Mali has been making in terms of both democratic reform and economic reform".
Soon after he took office in 1993, Christopher promised that the Clinton administration would make Africa a high priority and give it the attention it deserves.
Officials say Christopher has been unable to get to sub-Saharan Africa until now because of the pressure of other business, including Bosnia and Middle East peace negotiations.

The timing of the visit ahead of the November 5 U.S. presidential election could give President Bill Clinton -- already ahead of Republican challenger Bob Dole in public opinion polls -- an extra boost among Afro-American voters.
Other senior U.S. officials have been to sub-Saharan Africa in recent years, however, including National Security Adviser Anthony Lake and Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott.
Christopher and the administration have maintained that the United States is committed to engagement in Africa despite budget problems which have shrunk U.S. aid in recent years.

Christopher is due to hold talks on Tuesday with Mali's civilian president, Alpha Oumar Konare, an archaeologist and a historian by training. A meeting is planned with private voluntary organisations and Malian parlimentarians.
He will visit a U.S. Peace Corps water sanitation and tree planting project. Mali is the site of the Peace Corps' largest Africa mission, involving more than 200 people.
Christopher will return to Washington on October 14 or 15.
